extracted.intended_audience: government administrators, administrative analysts, management planners, and public-administration students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organizing, planning, executing, and controlling large administrative organizations (especially government agencies), including the roles of inspectors, regional officials, administrative analysts, and procedure divisions. Emphasizes functional authority, decentralization, delegation, and the division between program policy and administrative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation between regional officials and inspectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional Foresters and Supervisors need to cooperate fully with Inspectors, help plan their itineraries to include a cross-section of the Region, personally conduct them over large parts of the journey, and deal with Inspectors with complete frankness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors are expected to be equally frank, discuss reactions along the way, and inform the Regional Forester of the contents and conclusions of their report; regional officials should show both failures and successes to make frank inspection possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report review leads to actionable central guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: After inspectors' reports are written they are considered at length by the Chief and assistants; necessary elaborations are made, conclusions reached, and the Chief writes a letter to the Regional Forester transmitting the report and giving both general and specific instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Regional Forester usually answers, commenting on the report and outlining steps being taken to comply; the report and the Chief's letter then become the basis of general policy executed in the Region under functional supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist centralized clearance; promote corporate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the 'line of least resistance' of incomplete delegation and centralized clearance; instead build a sense of corporate responsibility and an instinct against overstepping authority or violating policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote self-control and minimize imposed control; maintain inspection and reporting so the central office stays informed, and use democratic participation in planning and observation to eliminate suspicion of dictatorship from above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized execution requires precise organization and no overlaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized execution and control 'after the fact' require a precisely built organization with no serious overlaps between fields of work and avoidance of conflicting orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve this by thoroughgoing voluntary cooperation between divisions because the Service's work consists of closely interlocking functions rather than discrete areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control should flow along functional lines rather than hierarchical lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Control in the Service flows along lines of authority which are functional rather than hierarchical: orders are a joint product formulated by various functional officers within whose spheres such work may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each functional officer carries authority and responsibility for his part; authority should arise from function — 'the man who possesses the facts should be the man who decides' — subject only to coordinating and precautionary control by superiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize needless reversion to higher officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks which can and should be done by subordinates should not be reverted to higher officials; sequences should consist mainly of operating steps with the minimum of control steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps top administrators' time free for developing policies and broad coordination and is key to consistent efficiency and quality of accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish program administration (what) from administrative management/procedure (how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative work divides into administration of program (the 'what') and administrative (procedural) management (the 'how'); both involve planning, execution, and control but deal with different problems and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program questions require subject-matter specialists; procedural questions demand administrative technique knowledge; both must be observed and staffed appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrators must combine technical knowledge and administrative skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative importance of technical training vs administrative ability varies with organization size, but in large organizations both technical and administrative knowledge must be brought to bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A professional administrator lacking technical knowledge can succeed if advised by specialists; a technician may succeed if administrative problems are solved by experts — ultimately either the person or a team must provide both kinds of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator should be a generalist on objectives and link to policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative objectives should be conceived in terms of the whole field of activity; administrators should be 'generalists' rather than merely specialists so they understand broader aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must be sound in terms of the technique of the activity involved; policy precedes administration, determines and evaluates it, and reshapes its purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear policy leadership to provide direction and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty and consistency of administration increase with definiteness of policy; lack of policy handicaps administration and leaves deputies eager for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practicable, policy should be broadened, detailed, and amplified to cover conjecture and speed administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation is necessary so administrators can perform higher functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators must delegate to free time for observation, consultation, analysis, study, and planning; allowing delegation of exercise of authority permits administrators to do essential higher-level tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when responsibility is delegated, administrators retain final responsibility but gain capacity to perform strategic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assistants: general staff vs administrative analysts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two classes of assistants: (a) general staff (extensions of the administrator's personality) who carry out routine detail contact with line divisions, and (b) administrative analysts (management planners) who are experts in administrative technique and plan administrative machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General staff handle routine implementation, guidance, and information; administrative analysts devise administrative structure, distribution, routing and timing of business, and methods of administrative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure divisions should emphasize organization and management over literary manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure or 'management planning' units should concentrate on organization engineering and administrative technique rather than merely polishing language and producing bulky procedure manuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good manual is an expression of sound administrative thought; procedure staffs should simplify routines, remove unnecessary operations, and plan facilities and methods rather than produce encyclopedic volumes of legalistic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of early procedure divisions (illustrative responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical functions include advising the Administrator on policy within scope; recommending standard procedures, forms, and instructions; devising or reviewing organization, methods, forms, and space arrangements; handling mechanics of creating and issuing material (charts, orders, instructions, forms); and drafting charts, graphs, maps, and pictograms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions may be delegated regionally as necessary for expeditious handling and originally focused on producing written material but should expand to include management planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative analysts should not formulate programs/policies or specify technical tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative analysts should not attempt to formulate basic programs and policies (the domain of legislature/board or administrators) nor specify technical details of line operations; they enter when organization and procedure for the program are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They advise on functional and hierarchical arrangements, plan channels for work flow, and arrange means for line executives to initiate, supervise, and control operations with minimum interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysts must observe operations and apply analysis by function, unit, and sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts should constantly observe the administrative machine, apply analysis by function, organizational unit, and administrative sequence, and study the relation of administration to operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should prepare data for planning necessary changes in structure and procedure so rearrangements can be made with minimal confusion; this maintains organizational balance and prevents waste, duplication, and poor human relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management planning units' principal responsibility (organization effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal responsibility is to study the effectiveness of the agency's basic plan of organization and develop improved plans to facilitate accomplishment of agency objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes proper division and functional distribution of work, establishment of sound authority and control structures, provision of appropriate staff facilities and services, elimination of jurisdictional conflicts, and proper program coordination to enable the chief administrator to energize and coordinate subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning offices need authority to conduct surveys and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective management planning requires grants of authority not only for planning itself but for the necessary surveys and investigations to permit thorough and well-grounded management planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Civil Aeronautics Administration example shows that authority for surveys and investigations enables planning units to perform comprehensive management planning rather than merely producing written instructions.
